questions.q: What does "encryption at rest" specifically protect?
options: Data that has already been permanently deleted
Data stored on physical media, like a disk or backup tape, rather than data moving across a network
Only data that is currently being typed into a form
Only network traffic between two cloud regions
questions.explain: Encryption at rest covers data sitting on physical storage media, as distinct from data in transit across a network.

questions.q: Which of these is true about encryption at rest on Azure and AWS today?
options: It is still an optional, extra-cost add-on that must be manually enabled on every resource
It only applies to data stored for longer than 30 days
Only AWS offers encryption at rest; Azure does not support it
Services like Azure Storage Accounts, Managed Disks, Amazon S3, and Amazon EBS are encrypted with AES-256 by default, with no setup required
questions.explain: Both major providers now encrypt most storage services by default using AES-256, without requiring manual setup.

questions.q: What is the real, specific threat that encryption at rest defends against?
options: A user forgetting their password
Someone gaining physical access to the underlying storage hardware, like a stolen drive or backup tape
An application crashing due to a software bug
A denial-of-service attack flooding a web server with traffic
questions.explain: Encryption at rest exists to make stolen or improperly disposed-of physical media unreadable without the key.

questions.q: Why can an attacker with a stolen but valid, authorized access key still read data that is encrypted at rest?
options: Because AES-256 can be reversed without a key
Because encryption at rest is only cosmetic and doesn't actually encrypt anything
Because stolen access keys automatically disable encryption at rest
Because the cloud platform transparently decrypts data for any request it considers authorized, regardless of whether the credential was stolen
questions.explain: Encryption at rest protects against physical access to hardware, not against someone who already holds valid credentials to the normal API or portal.

questions.q: Right now, who generates and manages the encryption key used for default encryption at rest?
options: The end user must generate it manually before any storage account can be created
A third-party certificate authority unrelated to the cloud provider
No key is actually used; the data is obfuscated instead of encrypted
The cloud provider, automatically, without the customer seeing or configuring it
questions.explain: By default, the cloud provider generates and manages the key entirely — this is the platform-managed key model covered in more depth in Lesson 11.
